firstComment:
Answer: it's not stone, it's a metal mix called ferrocerium 🔥

Inside a flint lighter, a small spring pushes a little rod (the "flint") up against a steel wheel with a rough, toothed edge.

When you roll the wheel, its rough edge scrapes tiny bits off the flint. The friction makes those bits hot.

Lighter "flint" is ferrocerium: a man-made alloy of cerium, iron and other rare-earth metals. Cerium catches fire at only about 150-180 °C (about 300-360 °F), so the hot scraped bits burn in the air. Those burning bits are the sparks you see.

Holding the lever opens the gas valve, and the sparks light the gas at the nozzle.

(Simplified 3D model, slowed down; real lighters differ in detail. Push-button lighters use a piezo spark instead of a flint.)

Sources:
Wikipedia, Ferrocerium (pyrophoric alloy of mischmetal: cerium, lanthanum, neodymium and other lanthanides, plus iron; struck with a harder material, friction produces hot fragments that oxidize rapidly in air, producing sparks; due to cerium's low ignition temperature, 150-180 °C; a hardened steel wheel strikes particles off the "flint"; used in cigarette lighters): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrocerium
Wikipedia, Lighter (ferrocerium, commonly called "flint", makes modern lighters possible; butane lighters combine the striking action with opening the valve; the spark ignites the gas): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighter
US Patent 5,509,799 (the spring urges the flint against the roughened surface of the striker wheel): https://patents.justia.com/patent/5509799

voiceover: Where does a lighter's spark come from?
Roll the wheel, and sparks fly out and light the gas.
Inside, a spring pushes a little rod, called the flint, up against the wheel.
The wheel's edge is rough steel, so as it turns, it scrapes tiny bits off the flint.
But the flint isn't stone. It's a special metal that catches fire very easily.
Scraping makes the bits hot enough, so they burn in the air. Those are the sparks.
The wheel scrapes the flint. The bits catch fire.
